It is true that this has been supplemented by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) lliis session by a quotation from a report made by a Jesuit missionary 200 years ago, wherein he had said that on a certain day in June, roses were in bloom and that they had no'night in that country. It is passing strange, Mr. Speaker, to observe the treatment that has been accorded by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to the various gentlemen who have held the portfolio of Railways and Canals in this government.
The gentleman who occupied that position from 1896 to 1903, Mr. Blair, the only practical man in Canada so far as railways are concerned, the gentleman who knew more about railways than all the other members of the cabinet put together, the gentleman to whom the Prime Minister gives a certificate of character to-day as being the best railway expert in the Dominion of Canada- his information was lightly treated, and he himself was so cavalierly treated, that he was not even invited in when the negotiations that led up to this contract were undertaken. It is true that that gentleman was not slow in expressing his opinion of this contract when it was up for consideration last session. He denounced it in no measured language claimed that it was a mere wilful waste of public money, utterly unjustifiable, without a single redeeming; feature. The hon gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Roche Marquette), in common with other hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken in this debate, seems to be very much alarmed at the extent of the liability the government is undertaking in connection with this railway scheme. They have placed the amount at something like $150,000,000. Now I do not intend to discuss that question, because it has been very ably dealt with by other gentlemen who have preceded me in this debate. I consider, however, that their figures are very greatly exaggerated. I desire to point out that the liability this country is to incur in regard to this railway measure will only arise in the event of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company turning out to be a financial failure. If that company turns out to be successful like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, it will not only pay working expenses and interest on the capital that will be invested, but it will also pay dividends to the shareholders who will invest their money in this scheme. If, I say, it turns out to be a scheme of that kind, then the liability of the country cannot arise at all. Now in order to ease the mind of the hon. gentleman who has preceded me, and of other hon. gentlemen who feel alarmed on this question, I wish to quote some authorities. I will quote from a source that they will not feel at liberty to question. The source I refer to is that of the leader of the opposition, in the speech he delivered on this question. I did not have the pleasure of hearing that speech, as I had not then the honour of a seat in this House. But I have given myself the pleasure of reading that speech, and I find that the leader of the opposition calls a number of witnesses to prove that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company has excellent financial prospects, and that it is likely to turn out to be a very successful venture, not only for the country but for the shareholders. These are the words the hon. leader of the opposition puts into the mouth of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson :
Passing as It will do through the most fertile and promising belt of country in the whole of the Northwest Territories, there cannot he the slightest doubt that this portion of the road, built, as I have said, under such favourable and economical conditions, will immediately produce excellent results, and will itself more than justify the adoption of the scheme in its entirety.
Further on he quotes Sir Charles as saying :
As regards the prairie section, the govern ment, not unfairly, held that it would he selfsustaining from the day of its completion, and in this view we are willing to concur.
Then we have a quotation from Lord Welby :

With the rapid settlement of the country, which will fellow the establishment of the line within a very few years, it will be a very profitable line.
Then we have an opinion from Mr. Hays :
Here is the Grand Trunk, the parent company, standing with a large traffic ready to deliver it west bound. This traffic is now given to a competitor. It does not have to wait five, ten or fifteen years to build up a traffic ; it starts with a traffic right from the beginning, and that is of a most remunerative character. This enterprise which we are advocating to-day, ladies and gentlemen, combines points and advantages that no other transcontinental line in the United States or Canada can have.
Now, Sir, these gentlemen, from whom the leader of the opposition quoted, are railway experts, they are men of very large experience in the management of Canadian railways, they have made a special study of the question for the purpose of embarking their own capital in the venture ; and it is especially gratifying to hon. members on this side of the House to have this point made so clear on such high authority as that of the hon. leader of the opposition. I do not think that the hon. leader of the opposition could have intended to make this point so clear to the House. He reminds me of an old Bible story. A prophet who climbed the mountain side and stretched forth his hand to curse the children of Israel. But instead of cursing them, ' behold he blessed them altogether.' He did not want to bless them, he wanted to curse them, but somehow when it came to the point he couldn't do it. Now we on this side of the House are especially grateful to the leader of the opposition for having made this point so clear. It completely relieves our minds of all anxiety in regard to our liabilities under this contract, in regard to the payment of interest on the bonds, in regard to the mortgage on the rolling stock, in regard to the receiver, and all these other bogeys with which hon. gentlemen opposite have endeavoured to frighten us in this debate. This measure, Sir, whatever may be said about it by bon. gentlemen opposite, is an attempt to do two things : To open up for settlement a very large section of country, some 3,000 miles of new Canadian territory, and to divert the trade of the west into Canadian channels and by way of Canadian ports. Now we all agree that this scheme will accomplish the first of these objects. It is admitted to be one of the greatest colonization schemes that was ever proposed in Canada ; and I submit, without going to the trouble to prove it, that it will also accomplish the second object better than any other scheme that is now available to the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at 6 o'clock, I was dealing with' the manifesto or memorandum of the 'exMinister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) addressed to the cabinet council in the fall of 1902. I do not intend to quote at any very great length from that memorandum, as it is now published in ' Hansard,' and has also been very thoroughly circulated throughout the country. But let me say, Sir, that the memorandum is important in this respect; that it points to a continuation of the policy which was adopted by this government in extending the Intercolonial Railway system to Montreal. We find from the memorandum that Mr. Blair proposed to continue the work of improving the Intercolonial Railway by extending it to the Georgian Bay, so that the government railway might share in the growing grain trade and carry western business to Canadian seaports. In return the country gets nothing save such benefit as will come from the building of a second transcontinental line. It will not become owner of the whole road even in case of default by the company, and it will have no greater control over the rates than it has, in the general law, over all roads. If the government is to assume all the cost of public ownership so-far as half the line is concerned, and three-quarters of that risk in the other half, it might better go the whole length, and build and operate the entire road, and thus secure for the people of Canada a transportation service at actual cost.
But there is no reason why the whole road should be built-at least just yet. Concerning the great stretch of country between Quebec and Winnipeg, Sir Wilfrid Laurier says he has ' mountains of information,' but it was an exceeding small hill he placed before the House. He told what a Jesuit missionary reported of the character of the country 200 years ago. That story is interesting, but it hardly affords a sufficient basis on which to spend $118,000,000 of public money. The time probably wil come when all the hinterland of Quebec and Ontario will be required to support our population ; but that time is not yet. The policy of to-day is to provide for the people of to-day ; to consolidate where development has already begun, rather than spread out over a vast area we are not yet in a position to effectively occupy. Looking at the matter in this light, as we think most reasonable men will, the proposal to leave the Winnipeg to Moncton line in abeyance, to extend the Intercolonial to Georgian Bay and thence to Winnipeg, meantime pushing the Winnipeg extension westward seems the wiser plan of the two now before the country. This plan would utilize Georgian Bay and Lake Superior-and it is over this magnificent water stretch the great bulk of western grain must be moved ; it would give us a second completed line from sea to sea at not more than the cost of building the Moncton to Winnipeg line, and it would give us public ownership of an all-across-Canada line-the only really effective means by which transportation charges can be controlled.
I admit frankly that the Intercolonial Railway has been badly managed by the hon. gentlemen. There is no question about that, and we have heard the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) tell us how badly it has been managed. But, notwithstanding all that, they made a profit last year of $130,000, leaving out the Prince Edward Island Railway, on which they made a small loss of some $72,160. Their percentage of expenses to earnings was a little high, 09-02 ; but under proper management-and there is no reason why it should not be managed, if we had a transcontinental government line, bv a commission, just as they are managing the Australian system of railways. There is no reason why the road should not be a great success and a great advantage to the people of Canada. We find Canadians going to other colonies and making a great success of railroads ; we find a Canadian at the head of a large system of railways in South Africa ; we find

a Canadian, Mr. Tait, in Australia, and wo have Canadians in our country who could manage our roads and make them a success.
I take very strong objection to the company having the revenue producing part of this line and the country having the nonproductive section. I feel, as the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) has stated, that the government are acting altogether too hastily in pushing 'the eastern section through an unsurveyed and unexplored district of country of which we know very little. There may be parts of it, and I hope there are, that wili turn out to be valuable country for agricultural purposes, bui we have millions of acres of land awaiting settlement that have never been, as X may express it, tickled by the plough. Let those lands be filled up before we consider-the advisability of building another line into that northern country for colonization purposes. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Wm. Roche) has dealt very fully with the weaknesses in the amended contract, tie has emphasized the fact that although the government advances practically all the money for tiie construction of that western road, they are powerless to foreclose their mortgage. The company may be in arrears for five years before anything can he done, and after that the government cannot foreclose, but the road passes into the hands of a commission, who operate it practically for the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and hand it back as soon as they have earned the fixed charges. I feel that there is nothing to prevent the company's western traffic going to American ports, and it is certainly decidedly in the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway that it should go to American ports. The hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy! lias pointed out that there is a difference of only 18 miles between the distance from Quebec to Portland and from Montreal to 1 ortland. What is to prevent the Grand Trunk Pacific from taking Canadian products from Quebec to Portland ? The 18 miles is only a trifle, it is a much shorter haul than to St. John or to the Canadian ports, and all they are bound to do is to give the same rate through Canadian ports ns they would give through American ports.
Now, Sir. Speaker, I am very strongly opposed to this scheme, and will have to vote against the resolution introduced by the hon. Prime Minister. Our aim, the aim of the Conservative party, is to make this Dominion of Canada compact, strong and prosperous, and I believe that aim will be carried out much better by the scheme proposed by the leader of the opposition than by the scheme proposed by the government.

The one great influence that brought this undesirable class of people to British Columbia was the construction of the British Columbia section of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Oriental labourers were brought into the province by the thousands from San Francisco. Now, Sir, it is very important for a British Columbia member to know just what the people of that province think of this railway policy. I can conceive of a member of this House having an opinion favourable to an abstract question, but that the demands of his constituents might force him legitimately to support a measure which in his own mind he might not be favourable to. I do not mean to insinuate that that is my position. I wish to say that I have looked into the question to my own satisfaction; that I have investigated as to the opinions of the people of my district; that I have taken an opportunity of testing the people of British Columbia on the question before the House, and ,1 have concluded to support the measure presented by the government, because I believe in it myself, and I believe that my action will be endorsed by the opinion of the people of British Columbia generally. I defy any member in this House to point to a. single complaint coming from British Columbia against this proposal, except in regard to the two matters I have mentioned. I have evidence here which will demonstrate to this House what the people of my province think about this scheme, as presented last session. Nay, more, I have the evidence, not of the friends of the Liberal party, but the evidence of the Conservative press'of British Columbia, in favour of the policy of the government. Last session when this question was being discussed here, my friend, Mr. Riley, from Victoria, repeatedly received letters and telegrams from the Conservatives of Britisli Columbia, requesting him to support the national transcontinental railway.
